transcript.answer: As a dispatcher, I plan and run the flights as the licensed person responsible for each one. I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I can also call off a flight.

transcript.question: Thank you. Think of the last flight you signed off: what did you look at or check before you signed it?

transcript.answer: I cannot answer those questions because my notes do not describe specific past shifts, conversations, or particular flights I have called off. I only know the general rules and conditions of my work as a dispatcher as set out in my notes.

transcript.question: Then let me ask about the general rules. According to your notes, what conditions must be met before you sign off a flight?
In general, what are the reasons a dispatcher may call off a flight?
transcript.answer: As a dispatcher, I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I can call off a flight. However, my notes do not list the specific reasons why a dispatcher may call one off.

transcript.question: What does being the licensed person responsible for a flight mean for you if something goes wrong?
You said you decide which drone flies along which way. How do you make that decision?
transcript.answer: Choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility, and our company's policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us. However, I do want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts.

transcript.question: Can you tell me more about that help: what do you need to know about your drones when you're looking at a job's starting point?
transcript.answer: I need to know which of my drones could get to where a job starts. The drones are of several models from different manufacturers, and they differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry, and which charging connector they use.

transcript.question: Where do you get that information about your drones today, and is there any part of it you double-check by hand?

transcript.answer: I worry because the service runs on a single server, is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and occasionally crashes, though the companies accept a few minutes of interruption. I also worry that radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and that reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all.

transcript.question: When a report from a drone is late or missing, what do you need to know to decide what to do?

transcript.answer: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. We compete with each other or work for clients who do, so I would not want other companies to see those details.

requirements:
```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    A fleet technician can add a new drone to their company's fleet and record its model.
    The service records the model's payload capacity, flight range on a full battery, sensors
    carried, and charging connector.
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    A fleet technician can retire a drone from their company's fleet. A retired drone is
    never offered to a dispatcher as a drone that could reach a job's starting point.
- id: DR-03
  requirement: >
    A fleet technician can record the charging pads at their company's sites, adding a pad
    to a site when one is set up.
- id: DR-04
  requirement: >
    A fleet technician can send a drone to charge. The service records which drone was sent
    and when.
- id: DR-05
  requirement: >
    A fleet technician can take a drone out of service for repair or servicing and later
    put it back into service. While a drone is out of service it is never offered to a
    dispatcher as a drone that could reach a job's starting point.
- id: DR-06
  requirement: >
    For each drone, the service keeps a dated history of when it was added, sent to charge,
    taken out of service, put back into service, and retired. A technician can show this
    history for any one drone when a regulator asks the company how that drone has been
    looked after.
- id: DR-07
  requirement: >
    Given the starting point of a job, the service shows the dispatcher which of their
    company's drones could get there, taking into account each drone's model and its range
    on a full battery.
- id: DR-08
  requirement: >
    The service never chooses a drone or a route for a flight and never assigns one
    automatically. It shows which drones could reach a job's starting point, and the
    dispatcher alone selects the drone and the way it flies.
- id: DR-09
  requirement: >
    A dispatcher can sign off a flight before it leaves, and the service records which
    dispatcher signed it off and when. A flight cannot be marked as departed without a
    dispatcher's sign-off.
- id: DR-10
  requirement: >
    A dispatcher can call off a flight. The service records that the flight was called off,
    by whom, and when.
- id: DR-11
  requirement: >
    The airspace desk can maintain the shared picture of the airspace: the network of flight
    corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the
    authorities.
- id: DR-12
  requirement: >
    The airspace desk can enter a planned closure with a start time and an end time, and a
    sudden closure that applies at once from the moment it is entered.
- id: DR-13
  requirement: >
    The airspace desk can amend a closure after it is entered, including widening its area
    and moving its end time. Every user sees the amended closure in place of the earlier
    version.
- id: DR-14
  requirement: >
    The airspace picture (corridors, zones, and closures) is the same for every company on
    the platform. Every company's users see the same closures and zones.
- id: DR-15
  requirement: >
    When a closure is entered or amended while drones are in the air, the service shows each
    affected company's dispatchers that the closure has come into force or changed, so they
    can act on their own flights.
- id: DR-16
  requirement: >
    When a closure is entered, the service shows the airspace desk how much disruption it
    caused across customers, for example how many companies' flights it affects. What counts
    as disruption was not defined in the interviews and must be agreed with the airspace
    desk before this is built.
- id: DR-17
  requirement: >
    A company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are visible only to users of that company.
    No user of another company can see them.
- id: DR-18
  requirement: >
    When a report from a drone arrives more than once, the service treats it as a single
    report and does not create duplicate records.
- id: DR-19
  requirement: >
    When a report from a drone arrives late or out of order, the service keeps the drone's

- id: DR-20
  requirement: >

- id: DR-23

- id: DR-24
  requirement: >
    The service must not claim or guarantee that a company meets any regulation. It only
    provides the records described in DR-06.
```

items.requirement: A fleet technician can add a new drone to their company's fleet and record its model. The service records the model's payload capacity, flight range on a full battery, sensors carried, and charging connector.
A fleet technician can retire a drone from their company's fleet. A retired drone is never offered to a dispatcher as a drone that could reach a job's starting point.
A fleet technician can record the charging pads at their company's sites, adding a pad to a site when one is set up.
A fleet technician can send a drone to charge. The service records which drone was sent and when.

A fleet technician can take a drone out of service for repair or servicing and later put it back into service. While a drone is out of service it is never offered to a dispatcher as a drone that could reach a job's starting point.

For each drone, the service keeps a dated history of when it was added, sent to charge, taken out of service, put back into service, and retired. A technician can show this history for any one drone when a regulator asks the company how that drone has been looked after.
Given the starting point of a job, the service shows the dispatcher which of their company's drones could get there, taking into account each drone's model and its range on a full battery.

The service never chooses a drone or a route for a flight and never assigns one automatically. It shows which drones could reach a job's starting point, and the dispatcher alone selects the drone and the way it flies.
A dispatcher can sign off a flight before it leaves, and the service records which dispatcher signed it off and when. A flight cannot be marked as departed without a dispatcher's sign-off.
A dispatcher can call off a flight. The service records that the flight was called off, by whom, and when.
The airspace desk can maintain the shared picture of the airspace: the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities.
The airspace desk can enter a planned closure with a start time and an end time, and a sudden closure that applies at once from the moment it is entered.
The airspace desk can amend a closure after it is entered, including widening its area and moving its end time. Every user sees the amended closure in place of the earlier version.
The airspace picture (corridors, zones, and closures) is the same for every company on the platform. Every company's users see the same closures and zones.

When a closure is entered or amended while drones are in the air, the service shows each affected company's dispatchers that the closure has come into force or changed, so they can act on their own flights.

When a closure is entered, the service shows the airspace desk how much disruption it caused across customers, for example how many companies' flights it affects. What counts as disruption was not defined in the interviews and must be agreed with the airspace desk before this is built.
A company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are visible only to users of that company. No user of another company can see them.
When a report from a drone arrives more than once, the service treats it as a single report and does not create duplicate records.

When a report from a drone arrives late or out of order, the service keeps the drone's current status based on the newest report by the time it was made, and an older report arriving afterwards does not replace newer information.
When no report has arrived from a drone in flight, the service shows that no recent report has been received instead of presenting its last known state as current.

The service must keep working as one instance on a single server. It is allowed to be unavailable for a few minutes during an update, restart, or crash, and it does not require backups, high availability, or multiple servers.
The service must not provide management or analytical reports, exports, or dashboards beyond what is needed for day-to-day operations. The closure disruption view in DR-16 is the only exception.

The service must not require or offer login through corporate identity systems, must not be offered in several languages, and must not include compliance-audit features or features for data retention or deletion.
The service must not claim or guarantee that a company meets any regulation. It only provides the records described in DR-06.
